tips.steak: Fat and protein ask for tannin: it makes the meat softer and the wine rounder.
tips.stew: Long-cooked meat is soft: the wine need not be tough, but warm and ripe.
tips.lamb: Lamb with rosemary and garlic is a classic with the Rhône and Bordeaux.
tips.game: Game likes a wine with some age: the earthy, mature notes find each other.
tips.barbecue: Smoke and sweet marinade call for a generous, fruity wine with some weight.
tips.burger: Juicy and savoury: a fruity red without too much tannin is the easiest friend.
tips.charcuterie: Salt and fat want acidity. A light red with fresh acidity cuts right through.
tips.chicken: The most obliging dish there is: white Burgundy or a light red, both good.
tips.duck: Duck with a fruit sauce? Then the wine may have some ripe fruit of its own.
tips.festive-bird: With many side dishes, a medium-bodied wine that overshadows nobody wins.
tips.pork: Pork sits between white and red: a full white or a light red both work.
tips.pork-belly: Fat shouts for acidity. A Vouvray or a dry Riesling makes it lighter.
tips.white-fish: The more delicate the fish, the quieter the wine. No oak, but tension.
tips.oily-fish: Salmon can take a light red: the one fish that welcomes Pinot Noir.
tips.shellfish: Oysters and Muscadet, or oysters and Champagne: salt against acidity, always good.
tips.smoked-fish: Smoke and a hint of sweetness in the wine make a surprisingly strong pair.
tips.fish-soup: Southern French soup, southern French wine. A firm Provence rosé is ideal.
tips.pasta-tomato: Tomato is acidic. A wine with less acidity tastes flat beside it, so go Italian.
tips.pasta-cream: Cream needs acidity as a counterweight, or it all gets too filling.
tips.ragu: A Chianti Classico with lasagne is a cliché because it simply works.
tips.risotto: Mushroom risotto can handle a light Nebbiolo too.
tips.pizza: Not a bottle to agonise over: fresh, red and Italian is enough.
tips.salad: Mind the dressing: the more acidic it is, the fresher the wine must be.
tips.roasted-veg: Roasting makes vegetables sweet and smoky: a wine with some spice suits them.
tips.mushrooms: Earthy seeks earthy. An aged Barolo with truffle cannot be improved.
tips.quiche: An Alsace Pinot Blanc is almost the standard answer here.
tips.pulses: Earthy pulses like a wine with a spicy, slightly rustic streak.
tips.veggie-burger: Look at the sauce and the spices: they matter more than the protein.
tips.sushi: Wasabi and ginger ask for a wine with a little sweetness as a buffer.
tips.thai: Hot and sweet: an off-dry Riesling cools the heat and holds its own.
tips.curry: Avoid firm tannin: it only makes spicy food sharper.
tips.chinese: Sweet-and-sour in the dish wants acidity and a touch of sweetness in the glass.
tips.hard-cheese: Aged Gouda with a tawny port is one of the best pairings there is.
tips.soft-cheese: Brie and Champagne: the bubbles wipe the fat away and wake the cheese up again.
tips.blue-cheese: Salt against sweet. Roquefort with Sauternes, Stilton with port: unbeatable.
tips.goat-cheese: Sancerre with crottin de Chavignol: same region, and you can taste it.
tips.chocolate: The wine must always be sweeter than the dessert, or it tastes sour.
tips.fruit-tart: Something sweet but with enough acidity to stay fresh.
tips.custard: Caramel seeks caramel: Sauternes or an old PX does the job.
tips.ice-cream: Moscato d'Asti with ice cream: low in alcohol, high in pleasure.
tips.aperitif: A dry fino sherry with olives and almonds is more Spanish than Spain itself.
tips.nuts: Amontillado and walnuts: both nutty, and they strengthen each other.
tips.fries: Bubbles and frying. It sounds odd and works fantastically.
tips.soup: With a creamy soup, a dry sherry works better than you would think.
tips.eggs: Oeufs en meurette with red Burgundy: one of the rare egg classics with red.
tips.spicy: Alcohol sharpens chilli. Choose a wine with a little less of it.

import.title: Bring your cellar over
import.subtitle: From the Wijnkelder app, with your bottles, spots, ratings and notes.
import.step1: In the Wijnkelder app, open its settings and make a backup. You get a small file.
import.step2: Choose that file here. First we only read it, and show you what would come over.
import.step3: Happy with it? Confirm, and your cellar is here in a moment.
import.privacy: The file is read on your phone. Only what is needed is sent, and only to your own cellar.
import.notJson: That doesn’t look like a backup file. Choose the .json file the Wijnkelder app made.
import.notWijnkelder: That file isn’t a Wijnkelder backup. Choose the file the Wijnkelder app made.
import.tooBig: That backup is too large to bring over in one go. Remove some old history in the Wijnkelder app and try again.
import.unplaced: {count, plural, one {# bottle has no spot yet} other {# bottles have no spot yet}}. You can place {count, plural, one {it} other {them}} later.
import.scaleQuestion: What were your old scores out of?
import.scaleHint: We worked it out from your scores. Change it if we got it wrong; everything becomes half stars.
import.nothingToBring: There is nothing to bring over
import.onlyOnce: Do this once. Doing it again would add everything a second time.
import.doneBody: {bottles, plural, one {# bottle} other {# bottles}} now in your cellar, {opened, plural, =0 {none} other {# more}} already opened, with {tastings, plural, =0 {no ratings} one {# rating or note} other {# ratings and notes}}.
import.tastingsSkipped: Your ratings and notes are waiting for one more database step before they can be kept. Everything else came over. The setup guide, “Updating the database”, shows what to do.
